name: Irritable bowel syndrome

matching.reasoningTemplate: Chronic abdominal pain with altered bowel habit and NO alarm features suggests IBS.

redFlags: Weight loss, bleeding or anaemia argue AGAINST IBS - investigate

clinicalPearls: Rome IV makes IBS a positive symptom-based diagnosis, not purely one of exclusion: recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day/week over the prior 3 months plus at least two of being related to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form, with onset at least 6 months earlier.
Rome IV is stricter than Rome III: it requires pain at least weekly and dropped 'discomfort' as a qualifying symptom; painless diarrhoea or constipation alone does NOT meet criteria.
Abdominal pain is mandatory for the diagnosis; it is typically episodic and crampy, often worsened by eating or emotional stress and relieved by passing flatus or stool.

Subtype by predominant stool form: IBS-C (constipation), IBS-D (diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed) - but subtypes are unstable, with about three-quarters of patients changing subtype and ~29% switching between IBS-C and IBS-D over a year.
Onset is usually before age 45 and IBS is two to three times more common in women, who make up ~80% of severe cases.

Symptoms commonly overlap with other functional disorders (fibromyalgia, headache, backache, genitourinary symptoms) and with functional dyspepsia, suggesting a shared, more extensive digestive disorder.

Bloating and a subjective sense of excess gas are common, but most patients actually generate a normal volume of intestinal gas and instead have impaired gas transit/tolerance and proximal reflux of gas.
Malnutrition is exceedingly rare in IBS and the pain almost always occurs only during waking hours, so sleep disruption from pain is unusual.
harrison.pathophysiology: IBS is a multifactorial functional bowel disorder with no structural lesion. Proposed mechanisms include altered GI motor activity (e.g., exaggerated postprandial and distention-evoked colonic contractions, increased high-amplitude propagating contractions with rapid transit in IBS-D), visceral hypersensitivity (lower thresholds to rectal balloon distention with sparing of somatic pain pathways), and disordered brain-gut interaction with central neural dysregulation (greater activation of mid-cingulate and prefrontal cortices on functional imaging). Psychological factors (anxiety, depression, somatization, prior physical/sexual abuse) modulate pain thresholds, and genetic factors such as serotonin transporter (SERT) polymorphisms are implicated. Peripheral contributors include low-grade mucosal immune activation with mast cells, lymphocytes and proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1beta, TNF), upregulated TRPV1 sensory channels, increased intestinal permeability ('leaky gut', chiefly in IBS-D and post-infectious IBS), gut dysbiosis (reduced microbial diversity, fewer Bifidobacterium/Faecalibacterium, more Enterobacteriaceae), abnormal serotonin pathways with increased enterochromaffin-cell serotonin in IBS-D, and bile acid malabsorption in up to ~25% of IBS-D.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease)
Gastroparesis or partial intestinal obstruction (postprandial pain with nausea/vomiting and bloating)
Acute intermittent porphyria and lead poisoning (painful constipation mimic)
Biliary tract disease, peptic ulcer disease, intestinal ischaemia, and gastric or pancreatic carcinoma (for epigastric/periumbilical pain)
infectionMimics: Giardia lamblia or other intestinal parasitic infestation
additionalInvestigations: Complete blood count for most patients
Fecal calprotectin or fecal lactoferrin, and/or C-reactive protein, in IBS-D even without alarm features to help exclude IBD
Serologic testing for coeliac disease in IBS-D where population prevalence is >=1%
Stool examination for ova and parasites in IBS-D when parasitic infection is endemic or suggested by history (e.g., untreated water)
Colonoscopy when alarm features are present, symptom onset is after age 40, or symptoms fail to respond to standard therapy
Random colonic biopsies to exclude microscopic colitis if diarrhoea is persistent/chronic
Hydrogen breath test (or trial of a 3-week lactose-free diet) for suspected lactase deficiency
Glucose hydrogen breath test for suspected small-bowel bacterial overgrowth with excessive gas/bloating
Gallbladder ultrasonography for postprandial right-upper-quadrant pain
Upper GI radiographs or upper endoscopy when dyspeptic symptoms coexist
redFlags: First appearance of symptoms in old age
Progressive course from the time of onset
Anaemia, elevated sedimentation rate, or leukocytes/blood in stool
Family history of colorectal malignancy (lowers threshold for thorough evaluation)
pitfalls: Treating IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion only and over-investigating: few tests are needed when symptoms are typical and alarm features are absent, and unnecessary investigations may be costly and even harmful.

Missing organic disease in higher-risk patients: older age, rapidly progressive symptoms, or alarm features should prompt a thorough work-up to exclude IBD, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer rather than labelling as IBS.
Attributing bloating to excess gas when most patients produce a normal gas volume but have impaired gas transit.
Over-interpreting an abnormal hydrogen breath test, which can be positive simply from rapid small-bowel transit and does not reliably predict treatment response.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison classifies IBS by predominant bowel pattern under Rome IV into IBS-C (predominant constipation), IBS-D (predominant diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed constipation and diarrhoea); these subtypes are noted to be unstable over time. Overall symptom severity ranges from mild to severe with significant quality-of-life impairment, but no formal graded severity score is specified.
